idFeatures: Basal rosette of jagged 'lion's tooth' leaves, single hollow stem with milky sap, yellow composite flower, puffball seed head.
warning: Harvest away from sprayed lawns and roadsides. Several look-alike yellow composites exist but all in this group are non-toxic.
uses: All parts edible: bitter greens, flower fritters, roasted-root 'coffee'.
story: The same cosmopolitan weed grows in sidewalk cracks on five continents.

idFeatures: Round scalloped leaves with a crinkled edge, small pale 5-petal flowers, flat 'cheese-wheel' seed pods.
warning: Mild and safe; can be mucilaginous. Avoid plants from contaminated soil.
uses: Young leaves raw or cooked; seed pods nibbled; leaves thicken soups.
story: Kids have eaten the 'little cheeses' for centuries.

idFeatures: Low sprawling mats, small opposite egg-shaped leaves, tiny white star flowers, single line of hairs running along the stem.
warning: Confirm the single hairline and star flower to avoid spurges (which have milky sap and are toxic).
uses: Mild raw green for salads and pesto.
story: A tender winter green that fills Berkeley garden beds when little else grows.

idFeatures: Fleshy paddle-shaped leaves, smooth reddish stems, low spreading mat, tiny yellow flowers.
warning: Distinguish from toxic prostrate spurge, which has thin leaves and milky sap; purslane has thick juicy leaves and no milky sap.
uses: Crunchy lemony succulent, raw or cooked; high in omega-3s.
story: A weed in every Bay Area sidewalk crack that's a prized vegetable elsewhere.

idFeatures: Diamond/goosefoot-shaped leaves with a white mealy coating on new growth, upright stem often striped pink.
warning: Contains oxalates; cook large servings. Don't confuse with toxic nightshade seedlings.
uses: Cook like spinach; seeds are an edible grain (a wild relative of quinoa).
story: One of the most nutritious wild greens, dismissed as a garden weed.

idFeatures: Basal rosette of broad oval leaves with prominent parallel veins; tall slender seed spikes.
warning: Tough when old; best young. No dangerous look-alikes.
uses: Young leaves cooked; crushed leaf is a classic field poultice for stings.
story: Followed European settlers so closely it was called 'white man's footprint'.

idFeatures: Soft (not truly spiny) jagged leaves clasping a hollow stem, milky sap, small dandelion-like yellow flowers.
warning: Edges prickle but aren't dangerous; just a milder relative of dandelion.
uses: Young leaves raw or cooked, like a mild dandelion.
story: A weed so common most people walk past their lunch.

idFeatures: Leaves with a row of prickles down the underside midrib, milky sap, leaves often twisting to face vertically.
warning: Very bitter and mildly sedative when mature; eat only young leaves, sparingly.
uses: Young leaves cooked; the wild ancestor of cultivated lettuce.
story: Its leaves rotate edge-up to track the sun, earning it the name 'compass plant'.

idFeatures: Long lance-shaped leaves with wavy curled edges; tall stalk of papery rust-brown seeds.
warning: High in oxalic acid — eat young leaves in moderation and cook them; not for those prone to kidney stones.
uses: Young leaves cooked like a tart spinach; seeds ground as flour.
story: The rusty winter seed stalks are one of the easiest plants to spot from a moving car.

idFeatures: Small arrowhead-shaped leaves with two backward-pointing lobes; low growth in lawns and disturbed ground.
warning: Pleasantly sour from oxalic acid — a garnish, not a quantity green.
uses: Tart leaves brighten salads and sauces.
story: A lemony accent that grows in the scruffiest patches of grass.

idFeatures: Basal rosette of toothed leaves; thin stalk of distinctive heart/purse-shaped seed pods.
warning: The purse-shaped pods are the reliable ID. Best before flowering.
uses: Peppery young leaves raw or cooked; a mustard-family green.
story: Named for the little coin-purse seed pods lining its stalk.

idFeatures: Tall plant with lobed lower leaves, four-petal yellow flowers, slender upright seed pods.
warning: Highly invasive; harvest freely. No toxic mustard look-alikes locally.
uses: Young leaves and flowers as a peppery green; seeds for mustard.
story: The waves of yellow that wash over Bay Area hillsides each spring.

idFeatures: Lobed rough leaves; four-petal flowers in white/pink/pale yellow; constricted 'beaded' seed pods.
warning: None significant; a feral relative of the garden radish.
uses: Peppery leaves, flowers, and tender green seed pods.
story: Escaped gardens generations ago and now colors every spring field.

idFeatures: Fern-like leaves in a flat rosette, small pink five-petal flowers, long pointed 'stork's bill' seed pods that spiral.
warning: Mild and minor; mostly a forage curiosity.
uses: Young leaves and stems raw, mildly tangy.
story: Its corkscrew seeds drill themselves into the soil as humidity changes.

idFeatures: Square stems and whorls of narrow leaves, all covered in tiny hooked hairs that stick to clothing ('velcro plant').
warning: The clinging hairs are unpleasant raw — cook or juice; eat young.
uses: Cooked young shoots; traditional spring tonic and tea.
story: Toss a sprig and it sticks to your sweater — every kid's discovery.

idFeatures: Round disc-like leaf with the flower stem passing straight through its center; tiny white flowers.
warning: The perfoliate disc leaf is unmistakable; few problem look-alikes.
uses: Mild succulent green, best raw in salads.
story: Gold Rush miners ate it for vitamin C, and the name stuck.

idFeatures: Opposite toothed leaves, square stems, fine stinging hairs along stems and leaf edges.
warning: Stings raw — wear gloves to harvest. Cooking or drying fully neutralizes the sting.
uses: A prized cooked green: soup, pesto, tea.
story: Hides in damp shady East Bay canyons, waiting for bare ankles.

idFeatures: Trailing wiry stems, small rounded scalloped leaves, minty aroma when crushed, tiny white flowers.
warning: Confirm by the strong mint smell; gather only where it grows wild in shade.
uses: Fresh or dried leaves for a delicate mint tea.
story: San Francisco's original name — 'the good herb' — came from this little vine.

idFeatures: Lance-shaped leaves, deep green above and silvery-white woolly beneath; strong sage-like aroma.
warning: Aromatic and medicinal rather than a food; avoid in pregnancy. Use sparingly.
uses: Traditional tea and smudge; a culinary herb in tiny amounts.
story: Lines creek banks across the East Bay and figures heavily in Ohlone tradition.

idFeatures: Feathery leaves; cone-shaped greenish-yellow flower heads with no petals; pineapple scent when crushed.
warning: Confirm the pineapple smell. A petal-less chamomile relative.
uses: Flower heads make a sweet chamomile-like tea.
story: Thrives in the hard-packed dirt of paths, parking strips, and sidewalk cracks.

idFeatures: Distinctly three-sided (triangular) flower stem, drooping white bell flowers with a green stripe, strong onion/garlic smell.
warning: ONLY eat alliums that smell clearly of onion/garlic — this rule separates them from toxic look-alike bulbs. No smell, no eat.
uses: Whole plant as a mild wild onion/garlic.
story: An invasive that conveniently tastes like a free leek.

idFeatures: Feathery thread-like leaves, solid green stems, yellow flower umbels, strong anise/licorice smell when crushed.
warning: Resembles DEADLY poison hemlock — but hemlock has purple-blotched stems and a musty smell, never anise. If it doesn't smell of licorice, walk away.
uses: Fronds in salads, seeds as spice, prized fennel pollen.
story: A Mediterranean escapee that lines East Bay trailheads and BART tracks.

idFeatures: Round shield-shaped leaves with radiating veins, trailing succulent stems, showy orange/yellow/red trumpet flowers.
warning: None significant; a garden escape gone feral.
uses: Peppery leaves and flowers in salad; pickled seed pods as 'poor man's capers'.
story: Tumbles over Berkeley fences and hillsides in a riot of edible color.

idFeatures: Clover-like trifoliate leaves, bright five-petal yellow flowers, juicy sour stems.
warning: High in oxalic acid — a pleasant tart nibble, not a meal. Just a taste.
uses: A few stems as a sour snack or garnish.
story: A South African import that paints Bay Area hillsides electric yellow each winter.

idFeatures: Trailing thin stems, slender straight thorns, three leaflets, smaller tart berries.
warning: All local blackberries are edible; this native is just being crowded out by the Himalayan invader.
uses: Berries fresh or in jam.
story: The original Bay Area bramble, here long before the giant invasive arrived.

idFeatures: Huge arching canes, thick ridged stems with broad curved thorns, five leaflets, big sweet berries.
warning: Wildly invasive — harvest guilt-free. Watch the thorns.
uses: Eat by the handful; cobbler, jam, syrup.
story: A Luther Burbank introduction gone rampant; it blankets every East Bay creek and empty lot.

idFeatures: Large soft maple-like leaves, NO thorns, white papery flowers, soft red dome berries like a thimble.
warning: Berries are delicate and don't keep — eat on the spot.
uses: Sweet-tart berries fresh; young shoots peeled.
story: A thornless berry of shady hill trails, gone within minutes of picking.

idFeatures: Large lobed grape leaves, shredding bark, climbing tendrils, small dusty-purple grapes.
warning: Confirm tendrils and grape leaf shape to separate from toxic look-alike vines.
uses: Tart small grapes; young leaves stuffed like dolmas.
story: Drapes over East Bay creek willows and blazes red in autumn.

idFeatures: Large shrub/small tree, compound leaves, flat-topped clusters of tiny cream flowers, then dusty-blue berry clusters.
warning: Eat only the ripe blue berries and flowers, and only COOKED. Raw berries, leaves, stems and bark are toxic. Avoid red-berried elders entirely.
uses: Cooked berries for syrup/jam; flowers for cordial and fritters.
story: A keystone native whose flowers and fruit feed half the hillside's birds.

idFeatures: Evergreen shrub, leathery serrated leaves, dense clusters of bright red berries through winter.
warning: Berries are harsh and contain cyanogenic compounds raw — must be cooked/heated before eating.
uses: Cooked into a tart sauce or dried after heating.
story: The 'California holly' said to have given Hollywood its name.

idFeatures: Smooth deep-red branches, stiff oval gray-green leaves, urn-shaped pink/white flowers, small apple-like berries.
warning: Berries are dry and seedy; flesh only. A genus of many local species.
uses: Berries make a tart 'manzanita cider' and jelly.
story: Its name means 'little apple' in Spanish, and the berries taste the part.

idFeatures: Thorny arching canes, compound leaves, simple pink five-petal flowers, round red-orange hips.
warning: Remove the irritating inner seeds/hairs from hips before eating.
uses: Petals in syrup; hips (high vitamin C) for tea and jelly.
story: A scrambling native rose along trails and creek edges.

idFeatures: Flat oval green pads with spines AND tiny hair-like glochids; magenta fruit on the pad rims.
warning: The tiny glochids are the real hazard — burn/scrape them off thoroughly before handling or eating.
uses: Young pads (nopales) grilled; ripe fruit (tunas) raw or in syrup.
story: Naturalized from old garden and homestead plantings, it survives on sunny East Bay slopes and around abandoned lots.

idFeatures: Evergreen; small cupped holly-like leaves with spiny edges; gray bark; broad rounded crown.
warning: Acorns are bitter with tannins and must be ground and leached before eating — never raw in quantity.
uses: Leached acorn flour for mush and bread.
story: The defining tree of the East Bay and a staple food of the Ohlone for millennia.

idFeatures: Massive deciduous oak, deeply lobed leaves, checkered gray bark, long pointed acorns.
warning: Like all acorns, leach the tannins before eating.
uses: One of the preferred acorns for flour — large and relatively sweet.
story: California's largest oak; the elders of the valley floor.

idFeatures: Lance-shaped glossy leaves; crush one for a strong camphor-bay punch; tall tree in canyons.
warning: Far stronger than Mediterranean bay — use a fraction of a leaf. The vapor can cause headaches.
uses: A sliver in stews; roasted nuts are edible.
story: The 'pepperwood' of California canyons — one leaf scents a whole pot.

idFeatures: Striking smooth reddish-orange peeling bark, leathery oval leaves, clusters of orange-red berries.
warning: Berries are edible but mealy and best cooked; eat in moderation.
uses: Cooked berries for cider/jelly.
story: Its glowing copper bark peels away each summer to reveal smooth green underneath.

idFeatures: Compound leaves with many leaflets, round green husks staining everything brown, very hard dark shell.
warning: Husks stain skin deeply; the nut is small with a thick shell — more effort than a store walnut.
uses: Rich nutmeat once cracked; husks used historically as dye.
story: An East Bay native walnut, often the rootstock under orchard trees.

idFeatures: Evergreen tree, large leathery deeply-veined leaves with fuzzy undersides, clusters of small orange fruit.
warning: Eat the flesh; the large seeds contain cyanogenic compounds — don't eat them.
uses: Sweet-tart fruit fresh or in jam.
story: An ornamental street and yard tree all over Berkeley, its fruit mostly left for the birds.

season: Blossom late winter; fruit early summer
idFeatures: Small tree with early pink/white blossoms (often purple-leaved cultivars), round red or yellow cherry-sized plums.
warning: Eat the flesh; don't crack and eat the pits (cyanogenic, like all stone fruit).
uses: Tart-sweet little plums fresh, or cooked into jam.
story: Berkeley's ornamental plum street trees quietly drop edible fruit each June.

idFeatures: Large lobed 'fig-leaf' leaves, milky sap, soft teardrop fruit, often growing feral from old plantings.
warning: The milky sap is irritating to skin; only ripe soft fruit is good.
uses: Ripe figs fresh or dried.
story: Escaped figs grow wild along East Bay creeks and railway edges.

idFeatures: Evergreen, narrow silvery-green leaves, gnarled trunk, small green-to-black drupes.
warning: Raw olives are intensely bitter and effectively inedible — they MUST be cured (brine/lye/water) for weeks first.
uses: Cured olives; the fruit of countless old Berkeley street trees.
story: Mission-era plantings mean free olives line many an East Bay sidewalk.

idFeatures: Woody shrub, needle-like aromatic leaves green above and pale below, small blue flowers.
warning: Unmistakable by smell; just confirm it's a planting and not sprayed.
uses: Culinary herb, free for the snipping from countless landscaped beds.
story: The most abundant 'wild' herb in Berkeley is the one planted in every parking lot.

idFeatures: Smooth hairless stems with purple/maroon blotches, fern-like leaves, white flower umbels, musty mousy smell.
warning: DEADLY. Mistaken for fennel or wild carrot — the purple-blotched stems and lack of anise scent give it away. All parts are lethal.
uses: None — recognition only.
story: The plant that killed Socrates, and it's common in damp, disturbed Bay Area ground.

season: Year-round; red in fall, bare canes in winter
idFeatures: 'Leaves of three,' glossy and scalloped, often reddish; grows as a shrub or climbing vine.
warning: Causes a fierce urushiol rash. Even leafless winter stems trigger it — when in doubt, don't touch.
uses: None — recognition only. The most useful native to know on sight.
story: Ubiquitous in the Berkeley hills — Tilden, Strawberry Canyon, every fire trail.

idFeatures: Sprawling gray-green plant, large soft leaves, huge white trumpet flowers (often opening at dusk), spiny round seed pods.
warning: DEADLY toxic and powerfully hallucinogenic — every part. No safe dose. Do not handle and ingest.
uses: None — recognition only.
story: Beautiful and dangerous; its night-blooming trumpets are pure warning.

idFeatures: Large evergreen shrub, long leathery lance leaves in whorls of three, clusters of pink/white/red flowers.
warning: DEADLY. Among the most poisonous common landscaping plants — never chew leaves or use stems as skewers. Smoke from burning it is toxic too.
uses: None — recognition only.
story: Lines California freeways and yards precisely because nothing eats it.

idFeatures: Tall spike of drooping tubular purple/pink/white flowers spotted inside; soft fuzzy basal leaves.
warning: Highly toxic to the heart. The fuzzy leaves are sometimes mistaken for comfrey — never eat them.
uses: None — recognition only.
story: The source of the heart drug digitalis — medicine and poison in the same leaf.

idFeatures: Tall fast-growing weedy shrub, large glossy star-shaped leaves often red-tinged, spiky red-green seed capsules with mottled bean-like seeds.
warning: Extremely poisonous — the seeds especially. Never ingest any part. Included only so you can recognize and avoid it.
uses: None — recognition only.
story: A striking ornamental escaped into vacant lots and creek banks across the Bay Area.
